entities.name: Laodice II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Laodice II, queen of the Seleucid Empire, emerged as a pivotal figure in the turbulent third century BCE, primarily through her marriage to Seleucus II Callinicus (reigned 246–225 BCE) and her maternity of two subsequent Seleucid monarchs, Seleucus III Ceraunus and Antiochus III the Great. Born into a prominent family, possibly as the sister of Andromachus, her lineage strategically connected her to the broader Hellenistic aristocracy. Her influence, though often overshadowed by male rulers, was instrumental in the dynastic continuity and political intrigues that characterized the Seleucid realm during a period of intense external pressures and internal strife, particularly the Third Syrian War and the War of the Brothers.

Her life was deeply intertwined with the dynastic conflicts that plagued the Seleucid Empire following the death of Antiochus II Theos. As wife to Seleucus II, Laodice II bore the future kings Seleucus III Ceraunus (reigned 225–223 BCE) and Antiochus III the Great (reigned 223–187 BCE), thereby securing the direct line of succession. She is notably implicated, albeit with some historical ambiguity, in the political maneuvering surrounding her husband's campaigns, including his defeat by the Galatians at Ancyra in 237 BCE. Polyaenus's account, referring to her as 'Mysta,' suggests a queen actively involved in the fate of her husband, even during his captivity, highlighting her potential role beyond mere procreation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Laodice II's significance stems from her role as the wife of Seleucus II Callinicus and, crucially, as the mother of two subsequent Seleucid kings, including the formidable Antiochus III the Great, thereby ensuring the direct dynastic line during a period of immense instability and contributing to the empire's eventual resurgence under her son.
